summary: The draft is quantitatively rich on benchmark figures but systematically strips named identifiers — flags, config keys, headers, chart values — that the interim notes hold verbatim. Zero HTTP header names, zero Helm value keys, and only two CLI flags appear anywhere in 305 lines, even though the report's deliverable is a phased implementation roadmap. Two committed interim-note findings (the Active-Passive/Active-Active throughput decomposition; the coordinator architecture as a coordination-free fourth topology) are load-bearing for Rule 1 — the draft's self-declared first branch — and are either compressed to a single clause or absent entirely. One provenance problem: the tiered effort estimates are presented as flat facts when their own investigator labelled them calibrated judgment, and two audited absences are asserted without stating the search (one of which the interim note flags as incomplete).

findings.location: Section 7, Rule 1 (final sentence: 'the standalone chart silently injects a leader-election flag whenever replicas exceed one, which turns a four-replica deployment into one-replica throughput'), and Section 1 inventory row 'EPP high availability'
findings.issue: The single most quantitatively developed mechanism in the availability interim note — why Active-Passive gives zero throughput scaling and what Active-Active actually buys — is compressed to one clause with no numbers and no mechanism. Rule 1 is the draft's declared first branch and the whole 'availability selects topology' inversion rests on it, so this is the highest-value compression in the report.
findings.evidence: interim-report-availability-and-lifecycle-off-k8s, quoting docs/operations.md and config/charts/README.md: (a) Active-Passive scaling is flatly useless — 'scaling the replica count does not increase the overall EPP throughput capacity... as only the active replica handles requests'; (b) Active-Active scales near-linearly with published multipliers: 2 replicas = 2.0x, 3 = 2.7x, 4 = 3.5x; (c) the mechanism is that 'in active-passive mode only the elected leader passes its readiness probe; standby replicas answer the readiness gRPC service with NOT_SERVING on purpose, so they never become Service endpoints'; (d) Active-Active carries an explicit plugin constraint — 'you must only use active-active compatible plugins... Avoid plugins that rely on local in-memory routing state, as this state is not synchronized across replicas.'
findings.recommendation: Develop Rule 1's Active-Active branch to the depth the interim note supports: give the 2.0x / 2.7x / 3.5x replica-scaling figures against the explicit 'no throughput gain in Active-Passive' statement, name the NOT_SERVING readiness mechanism as the reason standbys are excluded from the Service endpoint list (this is what makes the silently-injected leader-election flag a throughput trap rather than a cosmetic one), and state the chart's own Active-Active plugin-compatibility constraint as a design obligation — the draft already argues the precise producer satisfies it via independent per-endpoint convergence, so the constraint strengthens rather than weakens its case.

findings.location: Section 7, Rule 1 ('If you need multi-replica availability, the tie-breaker is whether a small Kubernetes control plane is acceptable'), and Section 8 'Multi-replica caveats'
findings.issue: The availability interim note explicitly hands the orchestrator a fourth topology option and flags it as worth surfacing; the draft never mentions it. Rule 1 presents three branches (single instance / picker in-cluster / Active-Active behind an L4 balancer) as exhaustive when the interim note names a documented architecture that sidesteps the coordination question entirely.
findings.evidence: interim-report-availability-and-lifecycle-off-k8s, Boundary conditions: the trichotomy 'does not apply to... the coordinator-service alternative architecture [[llm-d-routerdocscoordinator_architecturemd-at-main-llm-dllm-d-router-github]], which is explicitly stateless and needs no inter-replica coordination at all — an available escape hatch worth flagging to the orchestrator as a fourth option not framed as HA in the docs because it does not need to be.' The same note's open questions log the caveat that it still calls out to an EPP per phase, so it likely does not eliminate the underlying EPP HA question.
findings.recommendation: Add the coordinator-service architecture to Rule 1 as a named fourth option, stated with the interim note's own hedge: documented as stateless ('any instance can serve any request, no coordination between them'), which is why it is not framed as HA, but it still fronts an EPP per phase so it relocates rather than removes the picker-availability question, and no source pairs it with file discovery. Cite the coordinator architecture doc note.

findings.location: Section 7, Phase 0 ('Stand up the shipped no-Kubernetes reference on two workers... using the published flag set' — the phrase 'using the published flag set' also appears in Rule 1)
findings.issue: A phase whose exit criterion is 'requests route end to end' points at a flag set it never reproduces, even though the corpus holds the complete verbatim invocation. The draft gives a YAML snippet for the discovery key but not the command that consumes it, so the roadmap's first executable step is not executable from the report.
findings.evidence: research/runs/llmd-router-nonk8s-backends-54b774/temp/evidence-digest.md, lines 268-269 (empirical, quoted): './bin/epp --config-file=/etc/epp/config.yaml --pool-name=file-discovery --pool-namespace=default --grpc-port=9002 --grpc-health-port=9003 --metrics-port=9090 --secure-serving=false --v=2', runnable identically as a container (ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-router-endpoint-picker) or as a binary built via 'make build-epp'. interim-report-topology-and-k8s-shims additionally quotes discovery.md's worked example invocation 'epp --pool-name slurm-job-42 --pool-namespace slurm --config-file ...' against 10.0.0.1:8000 / 10.0.0.2:8000 vLLM instances.
findings.recommendation: Reproduce the reference flag set in Phase 0 with the port assignments (gRPC 9002, health 9003, metrics 9090) and note both delivery shapes (the ghcr.io endpoint-picker image or a make build-epp binary). Flag --secure-serving=false explicitly as a reference-config default that is a deliberate decision off-cluster, not a value to copy unexamined — it pairs directly with the Phase 4 metrics-auth obligation.

findings.location: Section 5C ('The code shows that description is engineering, not gloss') and Section 7, Phase 1 ('Enable the precise prefix-cache producer with per-endpoint discovery and pair it with the prefix-cache scorer by name')
findings.issue: Section 5C is where the draft says the thesis is won, and the KV interim note is its deepest packet — but the actual mechanism is paraphrased into arithmetic prose with every name removed. The strongest rhetorical asset in that note is that the config gate is literally named DiscoverPods / PodDiscoveryConfig and is nonetheless read only for two integers, which is exactly the kind of Kubernetes-sounding artifact a skeptic would cite as coupling. Phase 1 then tells the reader to 'pair it by name' without giving the key.
findings.evidence: interim-report-kv-event-path-off-k8s quotes extractor.go verbatim: the gate 'if !p.kvEventsConfig.DiscoverPods || p.kvEventsConfig.PodDiscoveryConfig == nil' is 'a config toggle the operator sets in the plugin's YAML params, not a code path that spins up ctrl.Manager or any Kubernetes client'; 'PodDiscoveryConfig survives... purely as a config carrier for SocketPort/EffectiveReplayPort() — it is read for two integer values, never used to open a Kubernetes watch'; the dial is 'port := p.kvEventsConfig.PodDiscoveryConfig.SocketPort + meta.GetRankIndex()' with 'zmqEndpoint := tcp:// + net.JoinHostPort(meta.Address, ...)' while the index/scoring key is the separate literal 'fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s", meta.Address, meta.Port)' appearing in three independent places. The producer.go source note gives the pairing key by name: 'Operators pair it with the generic prefix-cache-scorer (set prefixMatchInfoProducerName to this producer's instance name)'.
findings.recommendation: In 5C, name DiscoverPods / PodDiscoveryConfig and make the misnomer the argument: the only Kubernetes-shaped thing left on the flagship path is a config block's name, and the code reads two integers out of it. Give SocketPort + RankIndex as the dial formula and Address:Port as the separate index key so the two-identity-space claim is checkable. In Phase 1, name prefixMatchInfoProducerName as the key that must be set to the producer's instance name, since the stated failure mode (silent fallback to the approximate producer) is unavoidable without it.

findings.location: Section 7, Rule 1 ('using the chart's raw-configuration and volume-mount escape hatches') and Section 3D ('structured plugin configuration, raw configuration passthrough, and extra volume mounts make a hybrid topology reachable without forking the chart')
findings.issue: The hybrid topology is one of three Rule 1 branches and the interim note calls the chart escape hatches 'the load-bearing evidence for the hybrid branch' — but the draft names none of the three Helm keys involved, twice. A reader cannot act on, or falsify, a capability inference stated only as 'escape hatches'.
findings.evidence: interim-report-topology-and-k8s-shims, new-sources item 2, reading config/charts/README.md in full: 'router.epp.pluginsCustomConfig (additional raw ConfigMap entries keyed by file name)' and 'router.epp.volumes / volumeMounts (extra volumes for EPP pod)' together 'let an operator inject a hand-authored EndpointPickerConfig containing a file-discovery block plus mount a ConfigMap holding endpoints.yaml, entirely through documented values.yaml keys'; the absence side is equally specific — 'router.modelServers.matchLabels is required whenever inferencePool.create=true'. The same note flags the corroboration that file/plugin.go special-cases 'ConfigMap-style symlink swaps', which it reads as evidence the in-cluster-EPP-with-mounted-file shape was anticipated.
findings.recommendation: Name pluginsCustomConfig and volumes/volumeMounts where the hybrid branch is recommended, and name matchLabels-required-when-inferencePool.create=true as the specific absence they route around. Carry the interim note's corroborating point that the file plugin's deliberate handling of ConfigMap symlink swaps is affirmative evidence this shape was designed for — it converts the hybrid branch from bare capability inference into inference plus a design tell, which is the honest strength of the claim (the note is explicit that zero production deployments of this shape were found).

findings.location: Section 7, Rule 3 ('use a long-poll primitive where the registry offers one, such as a blocking query carrying the last-seen index with server-side health filtering') and Phase 3's tier costs
findings.issue: The plugin-design interim note's reason for splitting two tiers into three is that HashiCorp publishes the complete failure-mode checklist for blocking queries, which is what makes Tier 2 'barely more code than Tier 1'. The draft keeps the conclusion and drops the checklist, so the cheapness claim arrives unsupported. The Tier 3 correctness requirement is dropped outright.
findings.evidence: interim-report-custom-discovery-plugin-design: Consul's docs 'hand a plugin author the exact edge-case list to code against: reset the tracked index to 0 if a response's index is lower than the last one seen (raft snapshot restore or KV-list edge cases), sanity-check index > 0, and client-side rate-limit the loop (token bucket, burst ~2) rather than sleeping, since sleeping delays delivery', with the doc's own words 'the return of a blocking request is no guarantee of a change'; the health filter is named — '/v1/health/service/:service?passing=true... can be used to avoid additional filtering on the client side'. For Tier 3 the note requires 'reconnect-then-relist' be designed and tested explicitly, and calibrates it against production-stack's real K8s watch client whose reconnect is 'a flat catch-sleep(0.5s)-retry loop, not a sophisticated resync protocol' — 'good enough' is a lower bar than expected, but 'still risks silently missing events during a reconnect gap unless the plugin re-lists after every reconnect'.
findings.recommendation: Give Rule 3 the three named blocking-query edge cases and the ?passing=true server-side filter, so the Tier-2 cost claim is backed. Add the reconnect-then-relist obligation to the Tier-3 description as the specific correctness detail that has no test coverage anywhere in the evidence set, with production-stack's flat retry loop as the calibration point for how low the working bar actually is.

findings.location: Section 7, Phase 3 ('roughly 2-4 days of work, a long-poll variant adds 1-2 days, and a genuine persistent watch is 1-2 weeks'; 'The 1-3 week figure is the phase envelope')
findings.issue: Provenance discipline. These figures are presented in the same register as the report's measured numbers (the #1290 failure counts, the 151 percent throughput figure), but their own investigator labelled them explicitly as calibrated judgment with no reported basis. Under deep-inference posture a derived quantity must name what it derives from; here the derivation is expert estimate, and nothing in the draft says so.
findings.evidence: interim-report-custom-discovery-plugin-design, Confidence field: 'medium on the specific day-count estimates, which remain my calibrated judgment, not a reported number — no team in this evidence set has published effort spent building a from-scratch non-k8s EndpointDiscovery plugin for llm-d-router specifically.' The same note supplies the one thing that IS sourced and anchors the Tier-1 estimate: it is 'a near-mechanical transliteration of ~200 lines of already-reviewed, tested reference code'.
findings.recommendation: Label the tier costs as estimates rather than measurements, and state the anchor that makes the Tier-1 figure credible (roughly 200 lines of already-reviewed reference code to transliterate) alongside the fact that no published effort figure exists for this interface. The draft already handles vendor benchmark figures this way ('vendor-reported and not independently reproduced'); apply the same discipline here rather than letting judgment numbers borrow the authority of measured ones.

findings.location: Section 5E ('Explicit model selection already has a shipped header alternative documented as the substitute for the rewrite resource'; 'Tenant fairness is a bare header string defaulting to a standard flow'; 'The objective header names a Kubernetes resource')
findings.issue: The draft's chief piece of good news about lost policy inputs is that a shipped header already substitutes for the rewrite resource — and it never names the header. No HTTP header name appears anywhere in the 305-line report, so three actionable substitutions arrive unusable. This is the section the policy-inputs interim note spent its budget on, and the note's own framing is that these names are exactly what the width sweep failed to connect to the locus.
findings.evidence: interim-report-lost-k8s-policy-inputs, quoting the EPP HTTP headers reference: 'x-llm-d-inference-objective names an InferenceObjective resource in the same namespace as the InferencePool; EPP looks it up to apply priority/performance goals' (a name to resolve, not a raw integer — hence nil off-cluster); 'x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id... groups requests for fairness-based flow control; defaults to default-flow if omitted' — a plain opaque string with no CRD dependency at all; and 'x-llm-d-model-name-rewrite', documented as 'an explicit per-request override of the model name, an alternative to the server-side rule-based InferenceModelRewrite API'.
findings.recommendation: Name all three headers in 5E and carry the asymmetry the interim note calls out as its own triangulated finding: tenant fairness ships free off-cluster because its header is a bare string with a default-flow fallback, while priority dies because its header carries a resource name that must be resolved. That asymmetry is the reason exactly one plugin needs writing, which is the section's conclusion.

findings.location: Section 3C ('A repository-wide issue search for out-of-tree plugins returns essentially nothing') and Section 8 ('Package indexing reports no known importers for the runner or the framework interface packages as of 2026-09-11')
findings.issue: Two audited absences carry the precedent objection — the draft's own steel-man — and neither states what was searched. Worse, the extension interim note records that the most direct precedent check did not complete, which the draft's flat 'no known importers' assertion silently absorbs. Under deep-inference posture an audited absence must state its search; an incomplete search asserted as a clean absence is the specific failure mode.
findings.evidence: interim-report-extension-mechanism lists the seven queries run verbatim ('llm-d-router' 'cmd/epp/runner' import; github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/cmd/epp/runner site:github.com; 'llm-d-router' custom discovery plugin fork; 'llm-d-router' plugin.Register external; llm-d-router issues 'out of tree' OR 'out-of-tree' plugin; llm-d-router discussions custom plugin without fork; llm-d-router CONTRIBUTING.md 'third-party plugin' OR 'external plugin'), plus a direct CONTRIBUTING.md fetch ('16 lines, delegates to the org-level guide, covers only issue-claiming etiquette'). Its open questions then state: 'GitHub code search for cross-repo importers of github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/cmd/epp/runner hit an auth wall during the follow-up search and was not completed.'
findings.recommendation: State the shape of the absence search in 3C (a seven-query sweep plus direct CONTRIBUTING.md and issue-tracker fetches, two hits total, one of them an unrelated text match) so the objection's strength is auditable. In Section 8, qualify the importer claim: package indexing shows no importers and the authenticated code search that would settle it was blocked, so this is a strong absence rather than a proven one. The advocate posture is better served by a precisely-bounded absence than by an unqualified one a reader can puncture.

findings.location: Section 5D / Section 7 Phase 4 ('Enable metrics-endpoint authentication [[2061]]') and Section 3C ('Alpha plugins require an experimental-plugins flag')
findings.issue: Every security-relevant knob the report tells the reader to turn is described by function and not by name, including the one with a documented history of being silently disabled. Three flags the corpus holds verbatim appear nowhere in the draft.
findings.evidence: evidence-digest.md line 426: 'SSRF protection in the sidecar is opt-in (disabled by default) via --enable-ssrf-protection, and when enabled it watches a specific InferencePool CRD to build a host/IP allowlist from matching pods; requests to hosts outside the allowlist return HTTP 403.' Digest lines 236-237 and interim-report-availability-and-lifecycle-off-k8s on GIE PR #2061: the EPP carries a '--metrics-endpoint-auth' flag, and the chart previously emitted '--metrics-endpoint-auth=false' keyed off monitoring.prometheus.enabled rather than monitoring.prometheus.auth.enabled — 'real protection primitive; wiring was buggy until Jan 2026'. Digest lines 167-168: the gate flag is '--allow-experimental-plugins' (PR #2073, merged Aug 3 2026).
findings.recommendation: Name --enable-ssrf-protection where 5D says protection is off by default, name --allow-experimental-plugins at the Alpha gate, and in Phase 4 name --metrics-endpoint-auth together with the failure history: the flag existed but the chart wired it to the wrong value, so metrics auth silently went off whenever Prometheus was toggled. That history is the reason the obligation belongs in the standing list rather than a risk register.

findings.location: Section 7, Phase 4 ('Isolate the prefill hop at the network layer and turn on prefill TLS') and Section 7C standing obligations
findings.issue: The draft's standing security obligations cover the sidecar port and the prefill hop but say nothing about the KV-event channel, even though the draft itself establishes that the router dials outward to every backend's event port. The availability interim note logs a specific audited absence there that belongs in the obligations, not in silence.
findings.evidence: interim-report-availability-and-lifecycle-off-k8s, open questions: 'Does ZMQ KV-event transport (Centralized or Pod-discovery mode) have any authentication or encryption option (CURVE, TLS) anywhere in the llm-d-kv-cache codebase that the fetched docs simply did not mention? Both fetched docs (architecture.md, configuration.md) are silent on this — a real absence or an under-documented feature.' The draft's own Section 5C establishes the dial-outward requirement: 'the router dials outward to each backend's event port, so it needs reachability to that port and not merely to the serving port.'
findings.recommendation: Extend the network-isolation obligation to the KV-event port, stated with the absence's exact bound: two fetched kv-cache docs are silent on ZMQ authentication or encryption, so treat the event channel as unauthenticated until proven otherwise. Off Kubernetes there is no NetworkPolicy doing this implicitly, which is precisely why it is a standing obligation rather than a Kubernetes-parity gap.

findings.location: Section 7, Phase 0 ('Set the pool-namespace flag explicitly, since the fallback is a Kubernetes-flavoured default label') and Phase 2 ('Carry role labels if you plan on disaggregation')
findings.issue: Two Phase-level instructions are one specific short of being followable, and the draft omits a runtime reassurance that directly answers the silent-degradation worry it raises elsewhere.
findings.evidence: interim-report-custom-discovery-plugin-design: '--pool-namespace (flag > NAMESPACE env var > "default" fallback, per docs.md) is a different namespace — the router-instance-level pool identity used in metrics/logs — and must not be conflated with each EndpointMetadata.ID.Namespace, which is a per-endpoint grouping key defaulting to "default" in the file schema'; the same note cites roles.go for 'the closed set of llm-d.ai/role values the scheduler's P/D filters read from the generic label map'. interim-report-topology-and-k8s-shims quotes discovery.md: 'On bare metal, in Slurm, in Ray, or in any container without the Downward API, neither source is set and the pool is labeled default... Pass --pool-namespace explicitly', and notes the runner 'emits a one-time log at startup naming these inactive features — i.e. the degradation is self-documenting at runtime, not a silent trap.'
findings.recommendation: In Phase 0, give the resolution order (flag, then NAMESPACE env var, then 'default') and warn against conflating the pool-level namespace with each endpoint's own ID.Namespace, which is a separate per-endpoint grouping key. In Phase 2, note that role labels come from a closed llm-d.ai/role value set the scheduling filters read. Add the one-time startup log naming inactive features where the draft discusses what goes dark off-cluster — it is a concrete rebuttal to the silent-degradation worry and costs a sentence.
